summary: Toad Town was the heart of the Mushroom Kingdom. The capital. The center of culture, commerce, and governance. Now it's a contested ruin where three factions fight over rubble while the civilians who made it home have fled to wherever they could find safety. Waluigi grew up hearing stories about Toad Town's wonders. He never imagined he'd document its destruction.
description:
Waluigi visited Toad Town before the war. During the good days. When the biggest concerns were whether Princess Peach would appear at the summer festival and which team would win the annual Mushroom Cup tournament. Toad Town in peacetime was VIBRANT—colorful buildings clustered around the central square, mushroom-houses in every shade imaginable, residents who smiled and waved and actually seemed HAPPY to see you.

That Toad Town is gone. The physical structures might still stand—some of them, anyway—but the place that gave those structures meaning has been burned, bombed, and fought over until only the geography remains.

Pre-War Toad Town
Understanding what was lost requires understanding what existed. Toad Town before the war was a city built for joy. The architecture emphasized color, whimsy, and community. Mushroom-houses clustered in neighborhoods where everyone knew everyone. Public spaces encouraged gathering, celebration, and the spontaneous kindness that characterized Toad culture.

The central square—dominated by the fountain where Toads gathered for news, gossip, and public celebrations—served as the city's social heart. Markets lined the surrounding streets, selling everything from produce to handcrafted goods to those mysterious power-up items that Waluigi never fully understood but learned not to question.

Peach's Castle rose above everything else, its pink-and-white towers visible from any point in the city. The castle wasn't just the seat of government—it was a symbol, a landmark, a promise that someone was watching over the kingdom and keeping it safe. That promise turned out to be hollow, but while it lasted, people believed in it.

The city's infrastructure included an extensive pipe network—the famous warp pipes that allowed rapid transit between districts and, for the mechanically inclined, between dimensions. Waluigi used those pipes regularly during his athletic career, though he never felt entirely comfortable with the physics involved. You jump into a pipe in one location and emerge from a different pipe somewhere else, and nobody has ever satisfactorily explained how that WORKS.

The Fall
When Princess Peach vanished, Toad Town became the first battleground. The Toad Council attempted to maintain order, but their authority depended on Peach's legitimacy, and legitimacy is hard to maintain when the source has disappeared without trace.

The Peach Loyalists emerged from the castle's military garrison, claiming to defend the throne until the princess returned. Their definition of 'defense' expanded rapidly to include suppressing dissent, controlling movement, and establishing the authoritarian apparatus that Captain Toadette would later perfect.

Resistance began in the outer districts—neighborhoods where Legion influence was weaker and community bonds were stronger. What became the Liberated Toads started as block-by-block organizing, mutual aid networks that became mutual defense networks that became armed resistance.

Fawful's forces entered from the east, seizing the industrial districts and the pipe transit hub before defenders could organize. His mechanical troops didn't discriminate between Loyalist and Liberator—they attacked everyone, turning a political crisis into a three-way war.

The fighting damaged everything. The central fountain was destroyed in the first week—shelled by Loyalist artillery targeting Liberator positions nearby. The market district burned during street fighting when someone—nobody admits who—knocked over an alchemical supply stall and the resulting fire spread across three blocks. Peach's Castle was besieged, relieved, besieged again, and eventually partially collapsed when undermining operations compromised its foundations.

Current State
Toad Town in its current state resembles no city Waluigi would want to live in. The central districts are rubble. The residential neighborhoods are empty—civilians who could flee have fled, and those who couldn't have learned to hide. The pipe network is partially functional but dangerous, with some pipes leading to contested zones and others having been deliberately sabotaged.

Control of the city changes regularly. The Loyalists hold the castle ruins and the northern approaches. Fawful's forces maintain presence in the eastern industrial zone. The Liberators control pockets throughout the southern and western districts but can't consolidate. Combat is constant—not the organized battles of formal warfare, but the grinding attrition of urban conflict where every street corner is potentially hostile.

Infrastructure has collapsed. Water supply is sporadic. Power—the magical-mechanical hybrid systems that Toad Town relied on—functions in some areas and fails in others. The remaining civilian population survives through improvisation, trading, and the occasional mercy of whichever faction controls their block this week.

The Refugee Crisis
The destruction of Toad Town created a refugee crisis that has strained every surrounding region. Toads fled in waves—first the wealthy and connected, who saw the coming storm and left before it broke. Then the middle classes, when fighting reached their neighborhoods. Finally the poor and the stubborn, when even denial couldn't ignore that home had become uninhabitable.

The Vigilance—when it existed as a Liberator asset—served as a destination for many refugees. Temporary housing became permanent residence. The ship's population swelled beyond design capacity. When the Legion seized the Vigilance, those refugees became captives, and many of them died under Order 120.

Other refugees scattered across the kingdom and beyond. Sarasaland took some. The wilderness communities absorbed others. Some fled so far that they're effectively lost to Mushroom Kingdom affairs—starting new lives in places where the war is a distant rumor rather than daily reality.

Waluigi's Memories
Waluigi competed in Toad Town. Tennis tournaments in the public courts near the eastern gate. Go-kart races that wound through the streets while crowds cheered from mushroom-house windows. Dance competitions in the central square, with judges seated at the fountain's edge and the whole city watching.

Those memories feel like they belong to someone else now. Someone who lived in a world where Toad Town was eternal, where the fountain would always flow, where the castle would always rise above the skyline promising protection. That world ended, and Waluigi was too busy surviving to mourn it properly.

Waluigi mourns it now. Writing this entry. Documenting what was lost. The courts where Waluigi won his third amateur championship are rubble. The streets where he set his best kart time are contested combat zones. The square where he ALMOST won the regional dance competition—ALMOST, the judges were WRONG—is a crater.

Waluigi didn't love Toad Town the way native Toads loved it. Waluigi was always an outsider there, tolerated rather than welcomed. But he respected it. He enjoyed competing there. He appreciated that even a place that didn't fully accept him still gave him chances to prove himself.

Now there are no chances. Now there is only wreckage and war and the distant hope that someday, somehow, someone might rebuild.

Waluigi's Assessment
Toad Town cannot be saved in its current state. The physical damage is too extensive. The factional divisions are too deep. Even if the war ended tomorrow—which it won't—rebuilding would take decades and require resources that nobody currently possesses.

What CAN be saved is what Toad Town represented: community, culture, the belief that people can live together in something better than fear. Those things don't require a specific city. They require people who remember what peace looked like and are willing to work toward it again.

Waluigi is not optimistic about the Mushroom Kingdom's immediate future. But Waluigi has learned that optimism isn't required for action. You don't have to believe things will get better to fight for improvement. You just have to be too stubborn to accept that things will stay this bad forever.

Waluigi is VERY stubborn.

WAH. Someday there will be tennis courts again. Waluigi has to believe that, or what's the point of any of this?

summary: The Mushroom Regency is the provisional government that emerged after Princess Peach's death, and it operates exactly like you'd expect a government-by-committee to operate: slowly, carefully, and perpetually three steps behind factions that don't need quorum calls before acting. Every decision requires consensus. Every consensus requires meetings. Every meeting requires subcommittee reports. Meanwhile, the Iron Legion just DOES things, and the Peach Loyalists just FIGHT things, and the Regency is still forming a task force to discuss forming a response committee. Waluigi respects their intentions. Waluigi DESPAIRS at their speed.
description:
Waluigi needs to explain the Mushroom Regency because it's simultaneously important and frustrating, and both facts matter equally.

## Origin

When Princess Peach died—or vanished, or was assassinated, or whatever actually happened that nobody can agree on—the Mushroom Kingdom lost its center. Peach wasn't just a ruler; she was the SYMBOL that held everything together. Her authority legitimized governance. Her presence united factions. Her existence gave people something to believe in.

Without her, nothing held.

The Toad Council attempted to maintain order, but their authority derived from Peach. They were advisors to a monarch who no longer existed. Factions that had been suppressed or marginalized saw opportunity. The Peach Loyalists claimed to defend the throne. The Liberators claimed to represent the people. Fawful claimed whatever Fawful claims.

Into this chaos, the Regency emerged—an attempt to govern by committee what had been governed by crown.

## How It Works (Slowly)

The Regency operates through a council rather than a single leader. This sounds democratic until you experience it.

Every decision requires consensus. Not majority—CONSENSUS. Someone always has objections. Someone always needs more information. Someone always wants to table the discussion. By the time the Regency agrees on a response, the situation has usually evolved three times.

The council elects a president who serves as public face and ceremonial head. But the president's power is LIMITED by the council structure. They can represent, but they cannot command. They can propose, but they cannot impose. They can speak for the Regency, but the Regency has to agree on what they're saying first.

Waluigi has been on teams that required consensus. Waluigi's tennis doubles partnership with Wario technically requires consensus. It is MADDENING. You cannot respond to a fast serve with a committee meeting.

## The Fountain Visits

Every Regency president visits the Fountain of Dreams in Dreamland. Conspiracy theorists treat this as sinister. It's actually INFRASTRUCTURE.

The Fountain stabilizes dream-magic across the region. If leaders don't attune, nightmare phenomena increase everywhere. The visits are public. The ceremony is transparent. There's no secret loyalty oath to Dedede—if there were, Dedede wouldn't constantly argue with everyone who's already visited.

Waluigi has explained this MULTIPLE times in other entries. The Fountain is maintenance, not mind control. Please stop asking.

## What They've Actually Accomplished

Waluigi will give credit where due: the Regency's summit initiative produced results.

The Second Summit—despite everything that went wrong—created the Mushroom Kingdom Disaster Relief Program. Eight nations signed. Ships launched. Refugees received aid. This happened because the Regency did what committees CAN do well: build consensus, create frameworks, establish structures that survive individual crises.

The relief program kept operating even when delegations walked out of the summit. That's structural resilience. That's good design. That's the Regency's committee approach WORKING.

The problem is that building structural resilience takes TIME, and the Regency's enemies don't give them time. While they built consensus, the Iron Legion captured the Vigilance. While they established frameworks, Order 120 murdered prisoners. Good process doesn't help when your enemies operate faster than your procedures allow.

## Relationships With Other Factions

**Peach Loyalists:** Claim to fight for Peach's legacy but view the Regency as betrayal—committee compromise instead of royal continuation. Toadette's faction doesn't attack the Regency directly, but they don't recognize its authority either.

**Liberated Toads:** Work with the Regency because they need governmental recognition. The relationship is strained by response speed—or lack thereof. When the Vigilance fell, the Regency formed a committee. By the time they had recommendations, Order 120 had already happened.

**Iron Legion:** Treats the Regency as legitimate when convenient, obstacle when not. Files diplomatic notices before invasions. Somehow this is WORSE than just invading—it implies paperwork matters more than lives.

**Fawful's Forces:** Don't recognize the Regency at all. At least that's clear.

**Dreamland:** Complicated by the Fountain visits, Dedede's ego, and persistent conspiracy theories. The Regency needs Dreamland's cooperation for regional stability. Dreamland needs the Regency to stop believing internet rumors about mind-control fountains.

## Assessment

The Mushroom Regency is frustrating because it's ALMOST good enough.

The instincts are right: consensus-building, transparency, multilateral cooperation, structural resilience. These are GOOD values for governance. In peacetime, the Regency would function well. Boring, procedural, effective.

But this isn't peacetime. This is civil war, dimensional fractures, vampire politics, and factions that move at the speed of violence rather than deliberation. The Regency's toolbox was built for different problems.

Waluigi doesn't hate the Regency. Waluigi hates watching competent people fail because their systems don't match their circumstances. It's like watching a tennis player try to win a boxing match using tennis rules. They're good at tennis. Tennis is just the wrong game.

The question is whether the Regency can adapt before faster factions finish carving up the kingdom. Can they find ways to act quickly when needed while maintaining the consensus values they were built on? Can they be both deliberate AND responsive?

Waluigi is not optimistic. But Waluigi has been wrong before.

Once. About something minor.

The Regency's survival depends on proving Waluigi wrong again. Waluigi hopes they manage it.

WAH.

## Civil War Role

The Mushroom Regency is the legal-continuity claimant in the Mushroom Kingdom Civil War. It claims to be the government that survived Peach: the inheritor of offices, councils, guard structures, archives, fiscal systems, and law. This is not nothing. Legal continuity can feed people, pay soldiers, keep roads open, and decide which courts still recognize contracts.

But the Regency's legitimacy is damaged by the assassination lie. If Peach was murdered by an internal conspiracy and Bowser was blamed as cover, then the Regency did not merely inherit a crisis. It inherited the benefits of the crime. That is why the Peach Loyalists do not treat it as slow-but-lawful government. They treat it as the polished mask on a corpse.

Waluigi classifies the Regency as necessary, compromised, slow, and possibly doomed unless it can tell the truth faster than its enemies can weaponize it.

description:
Waluigi is writing about the Star Rod because it connects to the Fountain of Dreams, which connects to Dreamland, which connects to approximately half the conspiracy theories Waluigi has had to debunk in this encyclopedia.

## What It Does

The Star Rod grants wishes. That's the simple version.

The COMPLICATED version is that the Star Rod interfaces with the fundamental mechanisms of reality in ways that nobody fully understands. It connects to the Fountain of Dreams, which stabilizes dream-magic across the region. It connects to Star Haven, which exists partially outside normal dimensional space. It connects to the collective wishes of everyone in the Mushroom World, somehow aggregating and responding to mass desire.

When used responsibly—which means 'by the Star Spirits for legitimate wish-granting'—the Star Rod maintains cosmic balance. Wishes get granted in measured ways. Reality doesn't destabilize. Everything works.

When used irresponsibly—which means 'by anyone who steals it for personal power'—the Star Rod becomes a reality-warping weapon capable of fundamentally altering existence. Bowser stole it once and became effectively invulnerable until Mario sorted things out. Other theft attempts have been prevented, but the POTENTIAL for catastrophe keeps the Star Spirits vigilant.

## Connection to the Fountain

The Star Rod and the Fountain of Dreams are linked in ways that magical theorists argue about constantly. Some say the Rod powers the Fountain. Others say the Fountain channels the Rod. Still others say they're aspects of the same cosmic mechanism viewed from different perspectives.

What Waluigi KNOWS is that disrupting either affects the other. When the Star Rod was stolen, the Fountain's function degraded. When nightmare phenomena threatened the Fountain, the Star Spirits mobilized through the Rod. They're paired systems, and protecting one means protecting both.

This is why Dreamland's position as Fountain guardian matters. It's not just about one magical landmark—it's about an entire cosmic infrastructure that keeps reality stable. People who dismiss Dreamland as 'just sitting on a fountain' don't understand the SCALE of what that fountain connects to.

## Historical Incidents

The Star Rod has been threatened multiple times:

**Bowser's Theft** — Bowser stole the Rod, became invulnerable, conquered the Mushroom Kingdom until Mario restored it. Classic Bowser overreach.

**Nightmare Incursion** — A being called Nightmare attempted to corrupt the Fountain and Rod simultaneously. Kirby intervened. The fact that KIRBY had to intervene tells you how serious it was.

**Various Minor Attempts** — Smaller incidents that the Star Spirits handled before they escalated. Most people don't know about these because the Star Spirits are COMPETENT at security.

The pattern is clear: the Star Rod attracts people who want cosmic power. Those people must be stopped, or reality itself pays the price.

## Assessment

Waluigi is not qualified to analyze the Star Rod's metaphysics. Waluigi is a tennis player who got caught up in dimensional fractures, not a cosmic theorist.

What Waluigi WILL say is that the Star Rod represents the kind of power that should NEVER be pursued for personal gain. Waluigi has been tempted by power-ups and shortcuts throughout his life. Waluigi has usually resisted because Waluigi doesn't trust things that seem too good to be true.

The Star Rod is DEFINITELY too good to be true. Infinite wish-granting power? Reality manipulation? The ability to become invulnerable? There's always a cost. There's always a catch. The people who seek that kind of power usually discover the cost too late.

Waluigi will stick to tennis. Tennis has clear rules. Tennis doesn't risk unraveling existence.

WAH.

description:
Fawful has always been theatrical. The man cannot simply BUILD something—he has to build it dramatically, with unnecessary flourishes and self-aggrandizing design choices that serve no practical purpose beyond feeding his ego. The Fortress is Fawful's personality made architectural: bombastic, overcomplicated, dangerous, and somehow functional despite everything suggesting it shouldn't be.

The complex occupies a mountain valley in the eastern territories, far enough from the Mushroom Kingdom's core that Fawful could construct it without immediate interference. The location offers natural defenses—steep approaches, limited access routes—augmented by Fawful's own engineering. What was once a remote mountain pass is now an industrial nightmare.

Exterior Appearance
The Fortress is VISIBLE. Not just visible—AGGRESSIVELY visible. Fawful has constructed towers that serve no defensive purpose but ensure his flag flies higher than any surrounding terrain. The main complex is built in a style that Waluigi can only describe as 'evil carnival'—bright colors, clashing patterns, and architectural choices that seem designed to disorient anyone who approaches.

Smoke constantly rises from multiple industrial stacks. The air for miles around smells of metal and ozone and whatever chemicals Fawful uses in his manufacturing processes. Local wildlife has fled. Local vegetation has died. The Fortress has terraformed its surroundings into a wasteland that declares 'FAWFUL WAS HERE' to anyone unfortunate enough to wander close.

Defensive installations ring the perimeter: automated turrets, mechanical patrol units, sensor arrays that track movement across multiple spectrums. Approaching the Fortress without being detected is essentially impossible. Approaching the Fortress and SURVIVING detection requires either an army or the kind of luck that Waluigi doesn't trust.

Interior Organization
Intelligence on the Fortress's interior is limited—few people enter voluntarily, and fewer leave to share what they've seen. What Waluigi has gathered comes from intercepted communications, defector testimony, and the occasional captured Fawful unit with retrievable memory cores.

The Fortress appears to contain:

Manufacturing Levels: Multiple floors dedicated to producing Fawful's mechanical forces. Assembly lines churning out combat robots, maintenance drones, and the specialized units that Fawful deploys for particular missions. The manufacturing capacity is substantial—Fawful can replace losses faster than most factions can inflict them.

Research Facilities: Laboratories where Fawful develops new technologies. His mechanical innovations have outpaced everyone else's for years, and this is where that advantage originates. What exactly he's researching at any given time is usually a nasty surprise for whoever encounters the results.

Command Center: Fawful's personal domain, reportedly decorated in a style that defies description. Multiple accounts mention thrones—plural, multiple thrones in the same room—and portraits of Fawful in various heroic poses. The egotism is architectural.

Prisoner Facilities: The Fortress holds captives, though their fate varies. Some are kept for information extraction. Some are used in experiments. Some simply disappear. Rescue operations targeting the Fortress have been discussed but never executed—the logistics are too difficult, the defenses too strong.

Power Core: Whatever powers the Fortress, it's substantial. The facility's energy demands are enormous—manufacturing, defense systems, climate control, Fawful's personal quarters probably have seventeen different lighting schemes—and something has to meet those demands. Reports suggest a centralized power core in the lower levels, though its exact nature is unknown.

Fawful's Presence
Fawful reportedly spends most of his time in the Fortress, emerging only for major military operations or theatrical announcements. His management style is hands-on and micromanaging—he reportedly reviews production quotas personally, adjusts manufacturing specifications, and delivers lengthy speeches to his mechanical workforce despite them lacking the capacity to appreciate rhetoric.

The Fortress is an extension of Fawful's personality in ways that go beyond architecture. It reflects his obsessions, his paranoia, his overwhelming need to be acknowledged as the most brilliant mind in any room. Defeating Fawful probably requires destroying the Fortress, and destroying the Fortress probably requires defeating Fawful. The two are inseparable.

Strategic Significance
The Fortress is Fawful's center of gravity. His mechanical armies flow from it. His strategies originate from it. His ability to sustain operations depends on its continued function. Neutralizing the Fortress would cripple Fawful's war-making capability more effectively than any battlefield victory.

This is why no one has attempted it. The Fortress is too well-defended. The approaches are too dangerous. The resources required would strip other fronts of desperately needed assets. Fawful chose his location well, or more likely stumbled into a good location while looking for somewhere sufficiently dramatic.

The Fortress remains active, producing robots and projecting threat across the eastern territories. Every day it operates, Fawful's strength grows while his enemies exhaust themselves against each other. It's strategically sound, even if it wasn't strategically planned.

Waluigi's Assessment
Waluigi is not going to assault Fawful's Fortress alone. Waluigi is not going to assault Fawful's Fortress with an army. Waluigi is going to stay as far from Fawful's Fortress as circumstances allow and hope that someone with more resources and less sense decides to do something about it.

Fawful is dangerous because he's brilliant, unpredictable, and completely detached from anything resembling conscience. His Fortress is dangerous because it turns those qualities into industrial-scale output. The combination is... concerning.

If Waluigi HAD to approach the Fortress—if circumstances absolutely demanded it—he would focus on the power core. Everything runs on power. Disrupt the power, and the manufacturing stops, the defenses weaken, the whole edifice becomes vulnerable. But reaching the power core would require penetrating multiple defensive layers, navigating a complex designed by a paranoid madman, and probably fighting approximately ten thousand robots.

Waluigi's tennis racket is good, but it's not THAT good.

WAH. Some locations you document because they're historically significant. Some you document as warnings. Fawful's Fortress is both.

description:
# THE ALPINE MOUNTAIN INN
### Audit of High-Altitude Refuge, 3-Ducat Lodging, and Maid-Armored Espionage
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General of Mountain Inns and Ridiculous Disguises

Located along the snowy ridges of the Mighdural Mountains south of Alpine Bank, **The Alpine Mountain Inn** is a timbered, hearth-heated refuge for travelers navigating the treacherous passes around the Regal Capital.

While most mountain inns are quiet establishments serving spiced cider and salted elk, the Alpine Mountain Inn has become an active intelligence node in the conflict between the Iron Legion and Disaster Inc. Waluigi has audited many taverns, but never one where heavy infantry knights attempt to execute search warrants while wearing frilly white housemaid aprons! WAH!

---

## 1. Architectural Layout & Amenities

### Hearth & Common Room
- **The Great Hearth**: A central stone fireplace burning aromatic cedar logs, providing life-saving warmth against the sub-zero blizzards howling outside.
- **The Front Counter**: Where the pragmatic innkeeper collects the standard room rate of **3 Midland Ducats** (or 3 gold equivalents) per night.
- **The Timber Rafters & Upper Corridor**: Winding wooden stairs leading to private rooms with thick iron deadbolts—vital for keeping out unwanted Imperial guests.

---

## 2. The Blizzard Refuge of Bones (Harvestide 1040 BF)

Following his escape from Alpine Bank—where he eavesdropped on Thornbury placing a 2,062-gold rope bounty on Archie Miser—Bones trudged through a blinding snowstorm until local Imperial mountain guards found him shivering and escorted him down to the Alpine Mountain Inn.

Bones paid **3 Midland Ducats** for an upstairs room and collapsed onto the bed, holding his stolen Mages' Guild ledgers close.

---

## 3. The Maid in Iron & The Blizzard Evacuation

The next morning, the inn became the scene of a bizarre Legion infiltration trap:
- **The "Housekeeping" Knock**: A heavy, clanking knock rattled Bones's locked door, accompanied by a squeaky, falsetto voice calling out, *"Housekeeping..."*
- **The Armored Maid**: Peering through the keyhole, Bones observed a six-foot-tall, broad-shouldered Iron Legion knight dressed in a frilly white lace maid's uniform stretched over a heavy steel breastplate, carrying a broadsword and plate gauntlets!
- **The Blacksmith Trap**: After hiding behind the wardrobe until the knight retreated, Bones slipped downstairs. The innkeeper recommended visiting a local blacksmith, but Bones's instincts warned of an ambush.
- **Evacuation into the Whiteout**: Spotting four Legion guards and Thornbury waiting in the snowy street, Bones slipped out the back door and fled into the raging blizzard toward the Arunedeal Goblin Camp, raiding an abandoned blacksmith cart along the pass to steal an iron breastplate. WAH!

# THE ARUNEDEAL GOBLIN CAMP
### Audit of the Mighdural Mountain Snow Tribe & Winter Coat Commerce
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General of Mountain Hospitality and Unsanctioned Camps

Perched on the freezing slopes of the Mighdural Mountains between the Alpine Mountain Inn and the colossal stone barrier of the Iron Legion Checkpoint Wall lies **The Arunedeal Goblin Camp**, home to the hardy Snow Tribe of Arunedeal.

In a region dominated by Imperial border patrols, Mages' Guild double-agents, and sub-zero blizzards, the Arunedeal goblins survive through thermal conservation, scrap metal salvage, and aggressive currency negotiation. Waluigi has audited many goblin settlements, but Naaook and his snow tribe deserve special recognition for their willingness to sell a winter coat to a shivering skeleton for 75 gold coins while standing in a snowdrift. WAH!

---

## 1. Geographical Location & Encampment Layout

### High-Altitude Mighdural Pass
The camp is positioned in a sheltered pine hollow along the northern pass leading out of the Regal Capital. Surrounded by jagged ice ridges and buried under three feet of snowdrifts, the settlement is intentionally difficult for Imperial cavalry to reach.

### Encampment Structures
- **Low Leather Tents**: Constructed from cured mountain-beast hides and reinforced with pine poles. The tents are low-slung to allow blizzard winds to pass overhead without ripping the canvas.
- **The Central Campfire & Outskirts Perimeter**: Where Bones cast *Create Bonfire* outside his tent to ward off the freezing wind while resting on straw mats.
- **Naaook's Supply Depot**: A storage hide containing fur-lined winter coats, wooden shields, and salvaged blacksmith scrap gathered from abandoned carts along the pass.

---

## 2. Naaook & The Economics of Winter Coat Trading

During the **Flight from the Alpine Inn & The Legion Wall Checkpoint** (Harvestide 1040 BF), Bones—having fled the inn without cold-weather gear to evade a Legion knight disguised as a frilly lace maid—encountered Naaook carrying frozen branches through the storm.

What followed was a masterclass in goblin retail negotiation:
- Bones requested a winter coat and wooden shield, offering **75 gold**.
- When Bones attempted to haggle the price down to **50 gold**, Naaook immediately deducted the wooden shield from the transaction.
- Bones instantly surrendered and paid the full **75 gold** for both items.

Waluigi notes that Naaook's pricing structure proves that the Arunedeal Snow Tribe understands supply-and-demand economics far better than half the merchants in Toad Town! When an unarmored skeleton is shivering in a blizzard, the price of a fur coat is non-negotiable.

---

## 3. The Fey Spirit Clearing & Elbow's Arrival

The peace of the Arunedeal camp was shattered hours later with the arrival of **Elbow**, a battle-worn toad mage with a purple-bruised eye, wearing iron armor and pteruges. 

When suspicious goblin warriors emerged with raised weapons to challenge the newcomers, Elbow tapped his gnarled green staff on the frozen ground. A swarm of tiny, glowing fey spirits erupted from the wood, darting through the camp like angry hornets and leaving hundreds of stinging cuts that sent the Arunedeal goblins fleeing into the dark tree-line.

Before departing toward the Legion Checkpoint Wall, Bones called out into the empty clearing: *"Goblin guy! If you're around here, thank you! You kept your word! Till we meet again!"*—a rare moment of honor between an undead infiltrator and a mountain goblin trader. WAH!

# THE LEGION WALL CHECKPOINT (MIGHDURAL PASS)
### Audit of the Imperial Mountain Barrier & Order 120 Quarantine
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General of Impassable Architecture and Border Walls

Cutting across the entire northern defile of the Mighdural Mountains stands **The Legion Wall Checkpoint**, a towering, stone-fortified military barrier that marks the absolute perimeter of Iron Legion control outside the Regal Capital.

Waluigi has inspected many defensive fortifications—from Bowser's lava-rimmed castles to the Aegis Command battlements—but the Legion Wall Checkpoint is unique in its cold, bureaucratic brutality. Designed not just to repel invading armies, but to filter, inspect, and quarantine every individual traveler moving through the northern snows, the Wall represents the physical embodiment of General Ironhand's **Order 120**. WAH!

---

## 1. Fortress Architecture & Mountain Defile Control

### The Great Stone Barrier
The checkpoint wall spans the narrowest gorge of the Mighdural pass, anchored directly into the granite cliff faces on either side. Thirty feet high and reinforced with spell-hardened mortar, the wall is impossible to bypass on foot without scaling sheer, ice-covered cliffs.

### Garrison Battlements & Iron Banners
- **The Upper Battlements**: Manned day and night by Legion crossbowmen and magitek spotters equipped with thermal-vision scopes. Banners of the Iron Legion whip violently in the mountain gale along the parapets.
- **The Inspection Gatehouse**: A double-portcullis iron gate where travelers are forced to present travel writs, submit to cargo searches, and convert foreign currency into Midland Ducats.
- **The Garrison Barracks**: Housing over 200 elite Legionnaires, including rapid-response cavalry squads ready to ride out into the snowstorms to hunt fugitives.

---

## 2. Order 120 & The Quarantine of the North

Following the breach of Aegis Command and the Planar Fracture at Raventree Manor, General Ironhand signed emergency orders transforming the Legion Wall Checkpoint into a sealed quarantine zone.

Under Order 120:
- All Toad citizens and unsanctioned magic users are subject to immediate detention and interrogation.
- Bounties issued by Mages' Guild quartermasters (such as Thornbury's 2,062-gold warrant on Archie Miser) are synced directly to the gatehouse inspection ledgers.
- Any attempt to bypass the gatehouse is legally classified as active treason against the Regal Empire.

---

## 3. The Flight of Bones & Elbow (Harvestide 1040 BF)

During the climax of the **Flight from the Alpine Inn & The Legion Wall Checkpoint**, Bones and the battle-worn fey toad Elbow trudged through deep snowdrifts from the Arunedeal Goblin Camp, intending to escape north through the mountains.

Upon reaching the ridge overlooking the pass, Bones crouched behind a frozen boulder and surveyed the colossal stone barrier and its hundreds of garrisoned troops. Realizing that a frontal assault against a fortified Imperial fortress was suicide, Bones whispered to Elbow: *"Bones is fine with fighting, but not losing."*

Turning their backs on the towering wall, Bones and Elbow aborted their northern advance and retreated back into the freezing wilderness to seek an alternate maritime route along the coast.

### The Fey Leaf on the Boulder
Before departing, a single, perfectly green, un-withered fey leaf—dropped from the spirits of Elbow's gnarled staff—was left pressed against the frozen boulder overlooking the checkpoint. Waluigi notes that a fresh green leaf in a sub-zero blizzard is a clear message to the Legion High Command: the northern passes are being watched by forces far older than their stone wall! WAH!

# MOUNT EBOT
### Audit of a Mountain That Exists Because of a Typographical Error
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General, Walupedia Editorial Board

Waluigi wishes to begin with the only sentence that matters, because everything else on this page is a consequence of it.

**Mount Ebot has one T. Mount Ebott has two. They are four hundred miles apart and they are not the same mountain, and there is a printing plate in circulation that does not know this.**

---

## 1. The Error Itself

The Old World Mapping Company's **Survey Series IV** chart of the Northern Reach carries, bottom right, a neat oval cartouche with a compass rose in it and the legend **CORRECTIONS ON APPLICATION**. Slightly north of centre it prints **MOUNT EBOT**.

Somewhere in the Company's composing room a clerk with cold hands set the type for *Ebott* and dropped a T, and the plate went to press, and the press went to market, and the market has been selling that plate ever since to expeditions who read the famous name, buy the chart, and fly north instead of east.

Waluigi has filed for the correction. The Company has not replied. Waluigi is not confident the Company still exists in any form capable of receiving a letter, which raises the interesting question of who is still printing from the plate.

> **The practical test — count the consonants before you charter an aircraft.** Mount **Ebott**: barrier, monsters, a king with a beard, an Iron Legion survey file. Mount **Ebot**: bones, razors, no treasure, and a bill.

---

## 2. The Approach and the Cave

The eastern face carries a near-permanent storm cell — rain in sheets, hail above two thousand feet, and a horizon that simply stops being a line. Roughly thirty feet up the face there is a black slot in the streaming rock, wide enough for a small aircraft and no wider, opening into a stone gallery some sixty feet deep with a floor of wet grit.

The gallery is survivable. It is not welcoming. Anything that comes in through the slot at speed will slide the length of the floor and lose its tail to the boulder at the back; anything that walks in will find the slope of scree below the slot moves when looked at.

---

## 3. The Sentry

A figure of roughly four feet holds the upper scree. Hooded or helmed — no observer has resolved which — with nothing under the brim that lightens when the sky does, and no breath in cold air.

It throws bones. Sharpened human femurs, dry and old, taken from the mountain rather than carried onto it, delivered with no windup at all. When pressed it does not flee: it stops occupying its position, with a soft fold of air and a smell like a struck match, and resumes throwing from eleven feet away on flat footing.

**It has never been heard to make a sound.** It withdraws entirely when the level ground is denied to it, and it does not pursue down the slope.

---

## 4. The Seams

The middle slope answers earthquakes by opening in three parallel seams, a foot wide, evenly spaced, running downhill — and pushing bones up through them along their whole length at once, the way a splinter is pushed out of a healing hand.

Within six hours the seams close, the mud goes smooth, and every bone is gone from the surface. Waluigi counted forty-one in a strip the size of a market stall on the ascent and found nothing at all on the descent, including a jaw with three teeth in it that he had specifically gone back to look for.

---

## 5. The Bridge

Ninety feet of mortared cut stone across a gorge, with a low parapet and proper drainage channels — an imperial-grade span built by people who expected to still be there in a century. Somebody improved it afterwards, and somebody is still servicing the improvements.

**Sixty razors** sit in machined slots along both parapets at knee and shin height, angled to catch a leg going forward. **Six brass nozzles** run beneath the deck, thumb-diameter, throats black with soot and smelling of lamp oil even in rain. **Six pale pressure plates** are set a fraction low in the stonework, graded by weight. After the span fires it **resets itself** with a series of small precise clicks and lies there looking like a bridge.

The threshold is heavy. A man of ordinary build can stand on a plate with his whole weight and the bridge will decline to consider him. Wario triggered every element of it and came off the far abutment on fire in three places, which established both the grading and the safe footprints.

---

## 6. The Plank

Past the bridge, where the path bends around a shoulder of rock, a hand-thick plank is bolted to two driven iron stakes. The lettering is burned in with a hot iron by a hand that got tired.

> **RIP — 4 MISSING HUMANS.** JAVIER. MIKAELA. DANIEL. And a fourth, burned in like the others and then greyed almost out of the wood: **PRINCE ALPHONSE.**

Three names are clean. The fourth has been worked over patiently with something soft and greasy until the burned grooves filled with grey, and can only be read at an angle against the light. Nobody burns a name into wood at that cost and removes it for tidiness.

The marker itself is ordinary practice — the Mushroom Treaty requires a party entering unmapped ground to leave the names of anyone it loses — which means somebody obeyed the paperwork on a hillside in the rain and then had second thoughts about exactly one entry.

---

## 7. The Staircase and the Summit

The last thousand feet are cut steps, two hundred and some of them, at least ninety worn into shallow dishes by centuries of traffic on a mountain that is supposed to be empty. Near the top, a squared niche the size of a lamp or an offering bowl is cut into the rock beside the stair, its rim carrying worn lettering in an unread alphabet and one **mason's survey index mark** of the type found on treaty-era boundary stones.

Someone official surveyed this mountain. Someone official cut a mark into it. And the chart that survey produced spells it with one T.

The summit is a cairn, a view of grey rain in every direction, and a second burned plank:

> **MOUNT EBOT — SUMMIT — 1,340 FT — NO FURTHER SERVICE**

There is no treasure. There has never been a claim of treasure attached to Mount Ebot by anybody. The claim belongs to the other mountain, and it arrives here by post. WAH.

description: **The Ruins of Rohan Hillfort: A Tale of Resilience and Decline** In the heart of the verdant fields that once belonged to the mobile oath-kingdom of Rohan stands a testament to time's relentless passage—the Ruinsof Rohan Hillfort. This hillfort, a cradle of ancient memory, was once a formidable bastion against invaders, yet now it lies in disrepair, whispering secrets of its past glory through cracked stones and overgrown roots. The hillfort is more than just ruins; it's the echo of Rohan’s resilience and its struggle to protect itself from encroaching threats. ### The Rise of Rohan Hillfort Long before the time of Eomer and his kin, the descendants of Eorl the Young, Rohan was a land in transition. As the kingdom adapted to the changing political landscape and the shifting tides of power, it became essential for the Rohirrim to fortify their borders against foreign threats. The Ruinsof Rohan Hillfort was born from this necessity, a strategic stronghold perched upon a hilltop that offered a panoramic view over the rolling fields below. The site’s geographical advantage was not lost on the Rohirrim; it provided them with an early warning system and a vantage point for launching counterattacks. The hill fort's design was both practical and symbolic—its walls were built to withstand sieges, while its towers stood as silent sentinels against encroaching dangers. The construction of the hillfort marked a significant turning point in Rohan’s history. It represented not only the physical defense of their lands but also the spiritual unity of the people. The builders infused the structure with ancient lore and rituals, imbuing it with a sense of purpose that would last for generations. As the years passed, the fort became more than just a place of war; it became the heart of Rohan’s culture, a symbol of their tenacity in the face of adversity. ### The Fortification Process The hillfort's construction was an elaborate and labor-intensive process that demanded both skill and determination. Stone was the primary building material, sourced from quarries located near the site. These stones were carefully selected for their durability and size to ensure they could withstand the rigors of war. Each stone was meticulously shaped by skilled masons, a testament to the Rohirrim's craftsmanship. The walls of the hillfort were thick, designed to with stand even the heaviest bombardment. The inner chambers housed the defenders’ living quarters, armories, and storerooms filled with supplies needed for prolonged sieges. The fort’s design was also influenced by the natural landscape; the uneven terrain provided additional defense against invaders who might attempt to breach the walls. The towers of Ruinsof Rohan Hillfort stood tall and proud, each one equipped with observation points that allowed scouts to monitor enemy movements from afar. These towers were not only defensive but also served as beacons for communication between different parts of the kingdom during times of crisis. The highest tower, known as the Watchtower, was a central point where messages were relayed, ensuring that all parts of Rohan received timely and accurate information. ### The Role in Defending Rohan The Ruinsof Rohan Hillfort played a pivotal role in defending the mobile oath-kingdom against various threats. summary: The grant Jack Miser earned rather than inherited: a fortified manor, three villages, a mill, a quarry and the road tolls between them, on the Regal Empire's Midlands periphery. Eleven miles of it, give or take the moor. It is the seat of the Order of Jack, the home of Wanda Miser and three of her children, and — measured against the empires this archive normally files — extremely small. That smallness is the point of the page.
description:
## Scale, Stated Plainly

Waluipedia's atlas is full of thrones, capitals, planar reflections and fortress-cities. Vellanet Rise is none of those. It is **a minor grant**: a fortified manor on a shoulder of high ground, three tenant villages below it, a mill on the river, a quarry cut into the ridge, and the toll rights on the road that ties them together.

A rider crosses it in a morning. A bad winter closes it twice. Its chief strategic value is that the road exists at all, and that somebody competent is now standing on it.

The archive is being deliberate about this figure because the alternative is worse. Jack Miser is a **lord of about eleven miles**, and every draft that quietly upgrades him to a realm makes the rest of his file dishonest.

## The Manor and the Yard

The manor is fortified rather than grand: a curtain wall a good siege engineer would call optimistic, a hall, a chapel with a Knowledge-Domain shrine that was not there before Lunaria started visiting, and a muster yard that is the only part of the estate built to a proper standard.

The yard tells you what the money went on. Stone underfoot, drainage that works, a smithy that is never cold, and stabling for far more horses than the household owns — because the order's mounted strength is the part of the roll that is real.

## The Villages

Three, named on the tenure roll and unremarkable on it: grain, sheep, gravel, and the mill. They pay the toll share, they raise the levy when called, and they have not been raided since the year the order stood up, which is the entire local argument for Jack's existence and the reason no one there cares what his muster roll says on paper.

## Who Lives Here

Wanda Miser keeps a set of rooms in the manor and, according to every account, keeps them exactly as plainly as she kept the last house. July, Spring and Hark come and go — funded, housed, and pointedly not enlisted. Jack's own quarters are next to the muster yard rather than over the hall, which is either humility or logistics, and Waluigi has stopped trying to establish which.

There is no room set aside for Archie. There is also no room given away.

## The Chapel, and the Two Villages That Do Not Use It

The estate's faith arrangement is the most interesting thing about it, and it is interesting for an unflattering reason: it is an unresolved problem that nobody has yet been forced to resolve.

The manor chapel is a **Silver Flame** foundation. That is not a choice Jack made. The Regal Lion swears its knights in a Flamekeep rite, the Order of Jack inherited the Lion's chaplaincy wholesale, and so the chapel on the shoulder keeps the Litany of Purification, funds a candle allowance, and reads the list of forbidden entities on Venerias like every other garrison chapel in the Midlands. Its congregation is overwhelmingly the garrison. The Knowledge-Domain shrine in the side aisle — Lunaria's, and not on any foundation document — is the only part of the building anyone visits voluntarily.

The **upper two villages keep the Lunar Cycle**, and have since before the manor existed. They keep it quietly, in the ordinary Midlands way: nobody howls at the moon within sight of the road, and the hill families come down for the mill and the market and go back up again.

The Church of the Silver Flame's standing edict on this subject is not ambiguous. *Edict of Purification: Inquisitors have free reign in allied territories.* The Rise is allied territory. Two of its three villages hold to a Primal Forces faith, which the compatibility register scores at **25 out of 100 against the Celestial Order** — the low end, "Minor Friction," well-meaning outsiders, ten per cent on ritual components, nobody burns.

Twenty-five is a survivable number. It is survivable because no inquisitor has come up the road and made it a question. The tenure roll records the upper villages as tenants. It does not record what they believe, and that omission is the single most deliberate piece of paperwork on the estate.

## The Order's Unwritten Instruction

The Order of Jack's chaplains are Flamekeep-ordained and receive one standing instruction that appears in no order book, no oath, and no muster return: **do not raise the Edict against a tenant of the Rise.**

Waluigi has confirmed the instruction exists from three separate serving chaplains, none of whom would put it on paper, all of whom described it in almost identical words. It is obeyed. It is also, strictly, a commander instructing ordained clergy to disregard a standing edict of their own church, which is a thing the archive would like everyone to notice is *not currently a crime only because nobody has filed it as one*.

Jack's position, when asked, was that the villages have paid the toll and raised the levy for four years and nobody has been raided, and that he was not going to be the man who arrived on a hill and made a neighbour into a heretic. It is a good answer. It is also an answer that assumes the person asking is him.

## Waluigi's Assessment

An honest little holding that runs well, protects its tenants, and would not survive contact with anything this archive normally files as a threat. Its defence is not its wall. Its defence is that it is too small to be worth the march — a security policy which works exactly until the day it doesn't.

And the thing that will end it will not be an army. It will be one inquisitor with a writ, walking up a road that is legally open to him, into two villages the tenure roll has been carefully vague about for four years. WAH.

name: Bowser's Mushroom Compound
region: Mushroom Kingdom (interior site, exact overworld position unfiled)
population: Garrisoned — Koopa troops; exact strength unfiled
climate: Volcanic; contained
status: Standing; entrance wall breached and lava-moat tunnel search filed after 18 Harvestide, 1035 BF
summary: The smaller of Bowser's known holdings: a walled volcanic annex inside the Mushroom Kingdom itself, run up through a warp-pipe riser to a lava bridge on the second floor, and drained below by a lava lake, a lava falls, and a calm moat at ground level. Waluigi ranks its hospitality below its parent castle's, which he did not think was physically possible. The later Garden Above the Fire search confirms the outflow and tunnel system did not just drain the compound; it hid Luigi long enough for the rescue to reach him.
description:
Waluigi had always assumed Bowser kept one address per kingdom out of vanity. The Mushroom Compound corrected him: a smaller fortification on Mushroom soil, close enough to the backroads that a man can drive to it in an evening and strange enough inside that the drive feels like the last normal thing that happened to him. The gate carries a security window and a guard with a button. The button opens the gate. Past it, a warp pipe rises to the second floor, where a stone bridge crosses open lava to a far ledge that holds exactly one furnishing: an axe in the stone, waiting for someone with a grievance and no plan. Below, the lava lake runs to a falls and spills out past the walls into a calm shore moat at ground level — the compound drains its own disasters outward, which is more than can be said for its owner. Neo Bowser City, by the guard's own account, is elsewhere, larger, and meaner; this place is the annex, and on the night of 18 Harvestide, 1035 BF, its entrance wall was burst open from the inside by a smiling man in blue overalls.

## The Lava-Moat Search

The lava bridge file left the compound owing the archive a search of the outflow. The Garden Above the Fire pays that debt: Wario's crew returned to the moat, took Kat and Ana's high-rock sighting seriously, and found Luigi alive in the volcanic tunnels beyond the falls. That search changes the compound from ambush site to rescue site too — the same drainage that nearly erased the truth preserved just enough of it to be found.

name: Dr. Toad's Star Hill Clinic

population: Small staff, anxious patients, and at least one doctor who insists Dr. Toad is his real name
climate: Cool hill air outside; lamplight, clean dressings, and antiseptic inside

summary: A small Star Hill clinic where Wario's crew carried Luigi after recovering him from Bowser's lava outflow. Dr. Toad diagnosed serious but treatable burns, possible trauma delirium, and a strict ban on adventuring that Luigi immediately looked offended by.
description:
Dr. Toad's clinic sits close enough to the Star Hill roads that a group can reach it from the volcanic passages while still smelling of sulfur. The place is not a hospital palace; it is a practical night clinic — white sheets, glass bottles, clean bandages, a front desk that can panic at the sight of Wario carrying a limp plumber, and a physician cheerful enough to survive Waluigi asking if his name is actually Dr. Toad. On the night of 18 Harvestide, 1035 BF, it became the first quiet room after Bowser's compound: Luigi on the table, Wario blocking the doorway, Mona explaining too fast, Ashley hovering through an open window, and Waluigi pretending not to stand guard.

**2 Aethel, 1035 BF — the night the hill got a new name.** Two weeks after Luigi was carried in, a helicopter came for him and never reached the door. It caught its skid on the parapet of the storehouse next door, laid its rotor across the chimney and came to rest on its side on the roof, where a cracked fuel line burned on the stone and lit the clinic red. In the main street below, a man in Luigi's clothes recited verse at a courier; the courier shot him; the man lengthened, the cobbles split, and something with teeth and an eye on a stalk came up through the road and looked around. The courier went through the clinic's front window and came out of the storehouse stairwell. The storehouse itself would not keep its length — its stairwell grew while two men climbed it — and three copies of the man in green watched them leave by the fire ladder. The clinic's private wing, its patient, and its doctor were never seen. The courier's word for the hill was 'rot-zone', said like a word he had been issued.

summary: Trinity General School is the Kivotos academy where the archive's newest campaign opens. Kivotos was already in the record as Remi Akamatsu's birthplace — Residential District Seven, 12th Harvestide 1026 BF — and as a calendar the archive already carries; Trinity is the first building in it the archive has actually been inside. The relevant room is Classroom 2-B, which on the day of filing received a new advisor and discovered, mid-roll-call, that its curriculum is attached to SCHALE.
description:
The archive has held Kivotos at arm's length for a long time. It appears in Remi Akamatsu's file as the place she was born and left, in the wallet data as the issuer of Kivotos Credits, and in `calendars.json` as a four-term academic year with a six-day week and no true rest day. What it has not had is an interior.

Classroom 2-B is that interior.

**The room**
Desks in rows, a window line along one side, a whiteboard at the front, and a back row that functions as a separate jurisdiction. There is a door that slides rather than swings. The fluorescent lights are positioned such that a student standing directly in front of them can throw a silhouette across the room, which at least one student has worked out and uses deliberately.

**What the room is for**
On the evidence of the filing: roll call, announcements, and the delivery of information the students were evidently not briefed on beforehand. The advisor's stated remit is discipline and scheduling. The actual remit, disclosed in the same session, is SCHALE — deployment rotations, sector assignments, and hazard response.

**The seating, which is politics**
The front row is contested and was claimed by force of arrival. The window seats are sociable. The far corner is occupied by a student whose desk is angled away from the room. The back row holds the two students who do not participate and watch everything. Nobody assigned any of this.

**Waluigi's note:** a school where the timetable is a deployment rotation is not a school, it is a staging area with homework. Waluigi has read the roll. Eleven names, one advisor, and not one of those children was told what they were enrolled in until somebody asked a question the advisor answered honestly. WAH.
notableFeatures: Classroom 2-B — sliding door, window row, contested front row, and a back row that behaves as a separate jurisdiction
The whiteboard, on which the advisor drew a sector map of Kivotos's eastern perimeter and wrote THE RESISTANCE in underlined block capitals
The advisor's clipboard — carried constantly, tapped twice as a tell, and the physical object the roll call was read from
Fluorescent light bank at the front, used by at least one student as backlighting for declarations

summary: Kivotos is the academy city Remi Akamatsu was born in and left, and it has been in the archive's data for far longer than it has been in its prose — a calendar, a currency, a birthplace on one character sheet. The roll-call filing at Trinity General School is the first time the archive has stood inside it. Governance runs through academies rather than a crown, coordination runs through SCHALE, and the city is divided into numbered residential districts and lettered operational sectors.
description:
Kivotos has been quietly load-bearing in this archive for a long time without ever being written up.

**What the archive already held**
`Reputation-Matrix2/data/calendars.json` carries `kivotos_academic`: four ninety-day terms, a six-day week whose days are named Study, Lecture, Club, Field, Exam and Rest, five exam void days called Founder's Break, and a leap day every four years called Kaiser Day. Remi Akamatsu's file gives a birthplace — Kivotos, Residential District Seven, 12th Harvestide 1026 BF — and a wallet that carries Kivotos Credits, Credsticks and Data Chits alongside Midland Ducats. A city with its own calendar, its own money and an emigrant in the party is not a background detail.

**How it is organised**
Academies, not provinces. Trinity, Millennium and Shanhaijing are named in the calendar's `localTo` field as the bodies the academic year is local to. Remi's file names Gehenna Academy as a school she enrolled in and departed without formal withdrawal. The city is divided residentially into numbered districts and operationally into sectors; sectors 7 through 12 run along the eastern perimeter and hold warehouses, supply routes and abandoned industrial buildings.

**SCHALE**
Strategic Counter Hazard Activation League Execution. On the advisor's account it is the body that coordinates Knight deployments, allocates resources, and runs evacuation and hazard response — the difference, as he put it, between knowing there is a threat and doing something about it. It operates on a need-to-know basis. Student classes are attached to it, and at least one class did not know that until it was said out loud.

**The Resistance**
Described by the advisor, in the plainest terms he could manage for a room of confused students, as the bad guys: an internal threat operating from inside Kivotos, moving weapons through the eastern sectors. The archive records that as the advisor's characterisation and not as a finding. It is a one-sentence description of an armed political faction delivered to fourteen-year-olds, and no student in the room had the information to challenge it.

**The Equestrian question**
A diplomatic liaison programme exists between Kivotos and Canterlot — cultural exchange, small groups, intended to be quiet. Students saw liaisons walking the school openly. The advisor's reaction to being told this was not surprise at the programme but irritation at the breach, which is its own disclosure.

**Waluigi's note:** Kivotos has been sitting in this archive's calendar file for months like a folded map nobody opened. It has a six-day week with one rest day and the other five are named after work. Waluigi is not going to pretend that is subtle. WAH.

name: Fawful's Bean Badge
controllingFaction: Fawful (proprietor, 955 BF) — Mages' Guild operatives in the back room by the only account
status: Historical — trading in Efferd, 955 BF; no shop of the name trades in Toad Town in 1040 BF and the archive has not found the drain that reached it
summary: A bean shop in Toad Town with Fawful's name over the counter: jars of beans on the shelves, a tray of enamel badges by the till, and a cellar that connects to the warp drains under Peach's Castle closely enough that a lost ceremonial guard reached it from the dungeon in five hours with a letter for a map. On the one night the archive has it, the shop held the Koopa who was never locked in, two Mages' Guild operatives, a Goomba on a sack by the door, Fawful in a borrowed Guild cloak, and the plan for the vacuum shroom. Waluigi files it as a front, because a shop that a dead palace guard carried directions to in his coat is not selling beans.
description:
The Bean Badge is on the archive's map for one dawn. Everything below is from the account filed as [The Unlocked Cell](#/article/the_unlocked_cell_955_bf), which reached the shop through a grate and a cellar at about six in the morning in Efferd, 955 BF, and never left it on the record.

## The Shop

Small. Shelves of glass jars — beans, by the account, which did not inspect them — a counter, a tray of badges, lamps still lit against a grey window. A sign with Fawful's name on it, remembered by the account imperfectly. A Goomba sat by the door on a sack like a shop cat. The word *Badge* in the name is the shop's and not the archive's; what the badges were for, who wore them, and whether the tray on the counter was stock or a register are open.

## The Cellar and the Drain

John Lee came up into the shop from below — a grate, a cellar, the shop — after five hours in the warp system under Peach's Castle. The account does not map the route. It establishes that a route exists, that it runs from the palace dungeon to this cellar, and that it is navigable by a ceremonial guard with a lantern and no training, which means it was built to be navigated. The Koopa who left the dungeon ahead of him was already upstairs.

## Who Was In It

The Koopa prisoner, with the fat vial. Two Mages' Guild operatives — the people who told the father his son was being taken care of, and who asked him whether he was stupid for wanting an escort from people he had just said he did not trust. A Goomba. And Fawful, who put on a Mages' Guild cloak over the red to explain the vacuum shroom — inhaled, the Koopa King sucks up everything in reach, the brothers included; the castle's wards still active; *dispatch of this finkrat and takeover kingdom* — and whom the two operatives did not correct.

## Why It Is a Front

A dead palace guard in the hall of Peach's Castle had *meet me in Fawful's bean shop* in his livery before the shop had been mentioned to anyone. The Guild met there. The Koopa reported there. The plan was explained there. The archive has one bean shop in 955 BF that doubles as the Arrangement's back office and it is this one, and the archive would like to know what the Regency's first year did with it, because by 1040 BF nothing trades under the name and nobody in Toad Town remembers a bean shop with a cellar.

name: The Golden Land
region: Mushroom Kingdom (reached by wandering; overworld position unfiled)
controllingFaction: The King of the Golden Land — extinguished 20 Harvestide, 1040 BF
population: Small bright creatures that chirp and click; no settled folk filed
climate: Permanent midday glare; the light is brighter than the things it lands on
status: Failing — the palace at its centre came down on 20 Harvestide, 1040 BF, and its walls were seen peeling into white
summary: A shining country somewhere inside the Mushroom Kingdom, where the grass is thin shards of yellow metal, the trees ring like bells, and a friendly stranger in a red cap is always already waiting on the road. The one visitor on file walked in lost, was walked to a palace, and ran out of it with the sky coming apart behind him.
description:
Waluigi has been in a great many places that wanted something from him. The Golden Land is the first one the record shows that wanted nothing from a visitor — loudly, repeatedly, and in a voice that did not stop smiling. The road in is soft with welcome. Then the traveller looks down: the grass is not grass but thin shards of yellow metal, the trees chime when their leaves touch, and the ground in the mountain passes is polished so flat a man can read his own face in every step. Small coloured creatures play between the trunks and chirp louder when a guest declines to join in. Everything shines with an intensity the account calls blinding, and the account is written by a man who was squeezing a button in his pocket the whole way.

At the heart of the country stands [the Golden Palace](#/article/the_golden_palace), and the road, the creatures, the cheerful host and the mountains all lead there. That is the first thing to know about the Golden Land: it is one long approach. The second is what it does when the approach is interrupted. The service passages are plain stone, and the stone is not solid — it peels away in flat, untextured sheets with nothing behind it. When the palace fell, the sky above the country went grey in a streak that spread like a stain through water, the colours washed out of a flying ship, and the needles on its instruments turned to hand-drawn ink. Whatever the Golden Land is built from, it was drawn, and someone has a hand big enough to rub it out.

At the top sits a king made of light. It was the target of a Koopa raid, a trap for the raiders, or an ending nobody asked for — the account cannot decide, and the palace did not survive deciding.
description:
The palace is described in order, because the order is the point. A golden gate lowers with the groan of gold grinding on gold. A courtyard where the gates shut behind a guest with a finality that echoes off the walls. Marble stairs flecked with gold, a pair of massive ornate doors, a grand hall "that stretches so far into the distance it's hard to tell where the ground ends and the ceiling begins", torches that burn with no visible fuel, a double staircase, and at the top a set of doorbells that ring on their own. Beyond the largest doors, a throne of blinding light with a mountainous silhouette seated on it.

Every stage of the approach is built to make a visitor walk faster, and the host walked faster as it went on. The dining halls, the gardens and the good room for sleeping were promised on the way up; none were seen. The servants' passage behind a fallen pillar was seen, and it was the only part of the building that was honest: plain, dim, tight, and papered over a void.
